newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Global financier wins Kuwait parliament seat.
newsitem.headline: Global financier wins Kuwait parliament seat.

text.p: Results in Kuwait's second parliamentary election since the 1991 Gulf War started pouring in late on Monday with international financier Jassim al-Kharafi securing a seat.
Male supporters of the billionaire candidate exchanged kisses and danced in the street around Kharafi's house as fire works lit up the sky.
"Your Excellency, Speaker," chanted hundreds of supporters of the man who is widely expected to seek the job of speaker of the next assembly.
"This (election) is over, beware of the next," the crowd yelled but Kharafi, who has wide global holdings, refused to say if he would seek the speaker's chair.
"Later, later I will tell you tomorrow (Tuesday)," Kharafi, a former finance minister, told Reuters but his aides said he would seek the post.

Concerns over perceived renewed Iraqi threats and economic reforms to streamline government spending were the main issues in the election but many Kuwaitis were closely watching the outcome in Kharafi's race and in the fourth constituency.
Analysts say Kharafi could pose a serious threat to parliament speaker and veteran opposition leader Ahmad al-Saadoun in his bid to get re-elected as president.
Saadoun won in his constituency, one of 25, but the race for the speaker's chair could be a tough one. Kharafi opponents see him as a pro-government politician.
The outgoing, opposition-dominated parliament was no rubber stamp. It opened wide probes into alleged corruption and claims of poor government management before Iraq's 1990 invasion.

In the fourth district many Sunni Moslem Kuwaitis, slightly more than half of the 3,194 voters, are opposed to the controversial Hussein Qalaf, a Shi'ite scholar who traces his family tree to the Prophet Mohammad, voters said.
Kuwait's state television, which has been broadcasting live election reports all day, said Qalaf took one of the two seats in the constituency.
Jassem al-Mudaf, a Sunni, won the other seat while opposition veteran Abdulla al-Roumi and Ali al-Baghli, a former oil minister, failed to gain re-election.
"Sunni Kuwaitis don't want to see a turbaned Shi'ite scholar entering the assembly," said one analyst earlier. Shi'ites make up about 25 percent of Kuwaitis.
Left-leaning liberal Abdullah al-Naibari was also re-elected to the 50-seat parliament. He is a leading member of the Kuwait Democratic Forum (KDF) which is opposed to the government.
Unofficial estimates put the turnout in Monday's election at more than 80 percent of the 107,000 Kuwaiti men eligible to vote in the only parliamentary poll in a Gulf Arab state.
Police and military personnel, Kuwaitis under 21, those naturalised less than 20 years ago and women -- over 50 percent of the 700,000 Kuwaitis -- cannot vote.

Hundreds of women held gatherings on Monday to demand the right to vote. Some women waved banners reading: "Equality now", "Empowering women empowers the nation", and "We demand equality and justice".
Full results are expected to be announced early on Tuesday.

Many of the Islamist, liberal, independent, pan-Arab nationalist and pro-government candidates and their supporters are spending the night at their campaign headquarters closely watching television and contacting counting stations.
No incidents were reported in the relaxed voting atmosphere despite fierce election campaigns and bitter exchanges.
